title: Jeremiah 37:11–21
context: The narrator tells how, during the lull, Jeremiah set out for the land of Benjamin “to receive his portion there”; what that portion was is not stated, and some readers connect it with the family land in Anathoth (compare 32:6–15), though the text does not say so. At Benjamin’s gate the captain Irijah seizes him as a deserter. Jeremiah denies it, but the princes beat him and confine him in the house of Jonathan the scribe. King Zedekiah then brings him out and asks him secretly whether there is a word from the LORD; Jeremiah answers that the king will be handed over to Babylon, protests his own innocence, and asks not to be sent back. Zedekiah moves him to the court of the guard, where he receives bread while it lasts. Jeremiah 32:2–3 also places him in the court of the guard; the two accounts are named here without harmonizing their details.

verses.text: When the army of the Chaldeans had withdrawn from Jerusalem for fear of Pharaoh’s army,
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator returns to the time when the Chaldean army withdrew for fear of Pharaoh. Arminian readers note that the lull opened a window for travel, which Jeremiah used for his own affairs.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the narrator setting up the arrest within the same interlude described in 37:5. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as linking the political pause to the personal crisis that follows.

verses.text: then Jeremiah went out of Jerusalem to go into the land of Benjamin, to receive his portion there, in the middle of the people.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah sets out for the land of Benjamin to receive his portion there among the people. Arminian readers note that the prophet’s errand was ordinary, a matter of property or inheritance, though the text does not say exactly what.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise leave the portion unspecified, while some connect it with the field at Anathoth in 32:6–15. Both traditions read the verse without pressing a single explanation, and they note how quickly an ordinary trip turned dangerous.

verses.text: When he was in Benjamin’s gate, a captain of the guard was there, whose name was Irijah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Hananiah; and he seized Jeremiah the prophet, saying, “You are defecting to the Chaldeans!”
verses.arminianNotes: At Benjamin’s gate, the captain Irijah seizes Jeremiah, accusing him of defecting to the Chaldeans. Arminian readers see how the prophet’s public counsel to surrender made the charge seem plausible to those already suspicious.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the accusation as the hostility of those who rejected the word now turned on the messenger. Shared ground: both traditions read the arrest as a false charge against a faithful prophet, without guessing at Irijah’s motives.

verses.text: Then Jeremiah said, “That is false! I am not defecting to the Chaldeans.” But he didn’t listen to him; so Irijah seized Jeremiah, and brought him to the princes.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah denies the charge plainly, but Irijah will not listen and brings him to the princes. Arminian readers note the prophet’s honest protest and the captain’s refusal to hear, mirroring the nation’s refusal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene as a small picture of the larger story: truth spoken and not heard. Both traditions read Jeremiah’s denial as truthful and the arrest as unjust, recorded without exaggeration.

verses.text: The princes were angry with Jeremiah, and struck him, and put him in prison in the house of Jonathan the scribe; for they had made that the prison.
verses.arminianNotes: The princes are angry, strike Jeremiah, and imprison him in the house of Jonathan the scribe. Arminian readers see unjust suffering inflicted by officials who should have protected the innocent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet sharing in the sufferings that faithful witness can bring. Shared ground: both traditions read the beating and imprisonment soberly, as real injustice done to God’s messenger.

verses.text: When Jeremiah had come into the dungeon house and into the cells, and Jeremiah had remained there many days,
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah remains many days in the dungeon house and its cells. Arminian readers note the length of the confinement, a long trial that tests the prophet’s endurance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet’s patience under suffering, sustained though the text does not describe his inner life. Both traditions read the verse as recording hardship without dramatizing it, and they let the many days speak for themselves.

verses.text: then Zedekiah the king sent and had him brought out. The king asked him secretly in his house, “Is there any word from the LORD?” Jeremiah said, “There is.” He also said, “You will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon.”
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah secretly brings Jeremiah out and asks whether there is a word from the LORD; Jeremiah says there is: the king will be handed to Babylon. Arminian readers see the prophet’s courage in telling the truth to the one who holds his life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s word unchanged by the prophet’s suffering. Shared ground: both traditions read the secret meeting as showing a king who wants to hear but fears to act, and a prophet who will not soften the message.

verses.text: Moreover Jeremiah said to King Zedekiah, “How have I sinned against you, against your servants, or against this people, that you have put me in prison?
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah asks the king how he has sinned against him, his servants, or the people to deserve prison. Arminian readers see a fair appeal for justice, as the prophet protests his innocence before the authority.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that faithful suffering does not require silence about injustice; Jeremiah makes a lawful plea. Both traditions read the question as an honest claim of innocence addressed respectfully to the king.

verses.text: Now where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying, ‘The king of Babylon will not come against you, nor against this land’?
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah asks where the king’s prophets are who said Babylon would not come. Arminian readers see a pointed contrast: the false prophets’ promises have failed, while Jeremiah’s warnings are coming true.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as exposing false prophecy, compare Jeremiah 28 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the question as vindicating the true word over comforting falsehoods, and they let events confirm it.

verses.text: Now please hear, my lord the king: please let my supplication be presented before you, that you not cause me to return to the house of Jonathan the scribe, lest I die there.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah humbly begs the king not to send him back to Jonathan’s house, lest he die there. Arminian readers note the prophet’s vulnerability and his honest fear for his life, voiced without shame.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a godly use of lawful means to seek relief from suffering. Both traditions read the plea as showing that faithfulness and a desire to live are not at odds, and they note how the request returns in 38:26.

verses.text: Then Zedekiah the king commanded, and they committed Jeremiah into the court of the guard. They gave him daily a loaf of bread out of the bakers’ street, until all the bread in the city was gone. Thus Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah commits Jeremiah to the court of the guard and orders a daily loaf for him until the city’s bread runs out. Arminian readers see a measure of mercy from a king who would not fully side with the prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s provision for his servant through an unlikely means, sustaining him as famine closes in. Shared ground: both traditions read the daily bread as real care in dire circumstances, while the famine itself signals the siege’s grip.
